Every real dataset has problems. Some are mistakes, some are just how the data was recorded, and some only matter for certain questions. Cleaning means finding them, deciding what to do about each one, and keeping a record of how many rows each decision removed.

There's rarely one right answer. What matters is that you look, decide, and can explain why. That's exactly what you'll do in Section 2 of your workbook, and what your demonstrator will ask about at check-off 2.

On this page we'll clean the **total nitrogen** results for the Logan River at Yarrahappini. In your workbook you'll do the same for your own site and pollutant.

## 1. Load the data

Run this cell first. It loads the practical data into `conc`, just like P1, and sets the site and pollutant we're cleaning.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd

file = "data/yarrahappini_concentration.csv"
conc = pd.read_csv(file)

my_site = "145014A"
my_analyte = "Total nitrogen as N"
print(len(conc), "rows")
```

## 2. Look before you clean

Before you change anything, look at what's in each column. The `.value_counts()` method from P1 is the best tool for this, because it shows every different value and how often it appears.

```{pyodide}
print(conc["Site Code"].value_counts())
print(conc["Unit"].value_counts())
```

There are already two problems here. One site code has a space on the end, so Python treats it as a different site. And two results are in micrograms per litre, when everything else is in milligrams per litre.

```{pyodide}
print(conc["Operator"].value_counts(dropna=False))
print(conc["Quality Code"].value_counts())
```

Adding `dropna=False` makes `.value_counts()` count the blanks too. In the `Operator` column, a blank (shown as `NaN`) means a normal result. A `<` means the result was below what the laboratory can measure, and `IS` or `NR` mean there's no result at all. The quality codes 10, 20 and 125 are explained on the **Assessment Brief and Data** page on Canvas.

We'll deal with each of these in turn.

## 3. Stray spaces

Spaces at the start or end of a value are invisible when you look at the data, but they stop an exact match. The `.str.strip()` method removes them.

We'll make a copy of the data called `clean` and fix that, so the original `conc` stays as it was.

```{pyodide}
clean = conc.copy()
clean["Site Code"] = clean["Site Code"].str.strip()
clean["Analyte"] = clean["Analyte"].str.strip()
clean["Unit"] = clean["Unit"].str.strip()
clean["Operator"] = clean["Operator"].str.strip()

clean["Site Code"].value_counts()
```

Now there's only one site code. We tidied `Analyte`, `Unit` and `Operator` too, just in case. It doesn't hurt.

## 4. Pick your rows, and count what you remove

Next, keep only the rows for our site and pollutant, using the filtering from P1. Adding `.copy()` on the end tells pandas this is now a table of its own.

```{pyodide}
is_site = clean["Site Code"] == my_site
is_analyte = clean["Analyte"] == my_analyte
clean = clean[is_site & is_analyte].copy()

print(len(clean), "rows")
```

From here on, every cleaning step follows the same pattern. Store how many rows you had **before** the step, do the step, then print how many rows it removed. That gives you the record you'll need in your workbook.

```{pyodide}
before = len(clean)
# a cleaning step goes here
print(before - len(clean), "rows removed")
```

## 5. Quality codes

Here are the quality codes for our rows.

```{pyodide}
clean["Quality Code"].value_counts()
```

Code 10 means WQI's checks were done and the result is good. Code 125 is historic data with no confirmed quality checks. Which codes to keep is your decision. Here we'll keep only code 10.

The `.isin()` method checks whether each value is in a list. To keep codes 10 and 20, you'd write `[10, 20]`.

```{pyodide}
keep_codes = [10]

before = len(clean)
clean = clean[clean["Quality Code"].isin(keep_codes)]
print(before - len(clean), "rows removed")
```

## 6. Blank values and "<" values

Some rows have no result at all. The `.isna()` method finds blanks, and `.sum()` counts them.

```{pyodide}
print(clean["Value"].isna().sum(), "blank values")
clean[clean["Value"].isna()]
```

A row with no value can't be used, so we'll remove it. The `.dropna()` method drops rows with a blank in the column you name.

```{pyodide}
before = len(clean)
clean = clean.dropna(subset=["Value"])
print(before - len(clean), "rows removed")
```

Rows marked `<` are different. They do have a value, but it's the lowest level the laboratory can measure, not the real concentration. The real value is somewhere below it.

```{pyodide}
is_lt = clean["Operator"] == "<"
print(is_lt.sum(), "rows below the detection limit")
```

There are none for total nitrogen here, but there are for other pollutants. You have two reasonable choices. You can **keep** them, using the limit as the value, which makes those results a little too high. Or you can **drop** them, which loses your lowest results and pushes your averages up. Either is fine if you explain it. To drop them, you'd run this line.

```{pyodide}
clean = clean[clean["Operator"] != "<"]
print(len(clean), "rows")
```

## 7. Units

Earlier we saw two results in micrograms per litre. Let's see if one of them is ours.

```{pyodide}
clean[clean["Unit"] == "Micrograms/Litre"]
```

There are 1,000 micrograms in a milligram, so 1,450 micrograms per litre is 1.45 milligrams per litre. Left as it is, this one value is about 1,000 times too big, and it would drag the average for its season way up.

::: {.callout-warning}
One value in the wrong unit can change the answer to your whole analysis. Always check the `Unit` column.
:::

We can fix it rather than throw it away. The `.loc[rows, column]` notation picks out particular rows of a particular column, so you can change just those values.

```{pyodide}
is_ug = clean["Unit"] == "Micrograms/Litre"
ug_values = clean.loc[is_ug, "Value"]
clean.loc[is_ug, "Value"] = ug_values / 1000
clean.loc[is_ug, "Unit"] = "Milligrams/Litre"

print(clean["Unit"].value_counts())
print("Biggest value", clean["Value"].max())
```

## 8. Duplicates

An exact duplicate is a row that's identical to another row in every column. The `.duplicated()` method marks the second copy of each one. Adding `keep=False` shows both copies so you can compare them.

```{pyodide}
print(clean.duplicated().sum(), "duplicate rows")
clean[clean.duplicated(keep=False)]
```

The `.drop_duplicates()` method removes the extra copies.

```{pyodide}
before = len(clean)
clean = clean.drop_duplicates()
print(before - len(clean), "rows removed")
```

Note that rows with the same `Sample Reference` aren't duplicates. One water sample is tested for several pollutants, so its reference appears once for each.

## 9. Dates

The `Date Time` column is text, and the dates are written **month first**, the American way. So `7/6/18` is 6 July 2018, not 7 June. You can check this by finding a date like `10/24/17`, where the second number is bigger than 12, so it can't be a month.

The `pd.to_datetime()` function turns text into real dates. The `format` argument says how the text is laid out. Here `%m` is the month, `%d` the day, `%y` a two-digit year, `%H` the hour and `%M` the minutes. Adding `errors="coerce"` means any date that doesn't fit becomes a blank (`NaT`) instead of stopping your code.

```{pyodide}
fmt = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M"
dates = pd.to_datetime(clean["Date Time"], format=fmt,
                       errors="coerce")

clean[dates.isna()]
```

These are the rows that didn't fit. Look at them closely. They're written a different way, but they're still dates. Using `format="mixed"` tells pandas to work out each one on its own. Then `.fillna()` fills the blanks with those fixed dates.

```{pyodide}
odd = clean.loc[dates.isna(), "Date Time"]
fixed = pd.to_datetime(odd, format="mixed")
clean["Date"] = dates.fillna(fixed)

clean.loc[dates.isna(), ["Date Time", "Date"]]
```

Always check the fixed dates look right, for example against the `Sampling Year` column.

Last, check the earliest and latest dates. A date outside the monitoring period is a mistake.

```{pyodide}
print("Earliest", clean["Date"].min())
print("Latest", clean["Date"].max())
first_year = clean["Sampling Year"].min()
print("First sampling year", first_year)
```

These all look sensible for total nitrogen. If you ever find a date before the earliest sampling year, which starts on 1 July, you'd remove it like this.

```{pyodide}
first_date = "2007-07-01"

before = len(clean)
clean = clean[clean["Date"] >= first_date]
print(before - len(clean), "rows removed")
```

## 10. Month and season

The `.dt.month` attribute gets the month number (1 to 12) from each date.

```{pyodide}
clean["Month"] = clean["Date"].dt.month
clean["Month"].value_counts()
```

The wet season is October to March. We'll start by calling every row `"Dry"`, then change the wet months to `"Wet"`.

```{pyodide}
wet_months = [10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3]
clean["Season"] = "Dry"
is_wet = clean["Month"].isin(wet_months)
clean.loc[is_wet, "Season"] = "Wet"

clean["Season"].value_counts()
```

Finally, split the data into two tables, one for each season. These are what you'll compare in P3.

```{pyodide}
wet = clean[clean["Season"] == "Wet"]
dry = clean[clean["Season"] == "Dry"]
print(len(wet), "wet season samples")
print(len(dry), "dry season samples")
```

There are far more wet season samples. That's because WQI sample very often during floods and only monthly when the river is low. Keep that in mind when you compare the seasons.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_spot

```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_spot
name = "Particulate nitrogen as N"
pn = conc[conc["Analyte"] == name]

print(pn["Site Code"].______())
print(pn["Operator"].value_counts(______=False))
print(pn["Quality Code"].______())
```

All three lines use the same method, the one that counts how many rows have each value. The middle one also needs the argument that counts blanks.
:::

Use `.value_counts()` on the first and last lines, and `dropna=False` in the middle.

```python
name = "Particulate nitrogen as N"
```

What's wrong with the site code, and how many rows does it affect? How many results are below the detection limit? How many rows aren't quality code 10? For each one, what would you do?

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd
conc = pd.read_csv("data/yarrahappini_concentration.csv")
name = "Filterable Reactive phosphorus as P"
frp = conc[conc["Analyte"] == name].copy()
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_units
is_ug = frp["Unit"] == ______
print(is_ug.sum(), "rows to fix")

ug_values = frp.loc[is_ug, "Value"]
frp.loc[is_ug, "Value"] = ug_values ______ 1000
frp.loc[is_ug, "Unit"] = ______

print(frp["Unit"].value_counts())
print("Biggest value", frp["Value"].max())
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_units"}
The unit names are text, so they need quotes. Check the exact spelling with `.value_counts()` in section 2. A microgram is a thousandth of a milligram.

Compare with `"Micrograms/Litre"`, divide with `/`, and set the unit to `"Milligrams/Litre"`.

Run `frp["Value"].mean()` before and after the fix. How much did one wrong value change the mean?

### Activity 3. Dates and seasons

You'll need sections 9 and 10.

The **total suspended solids** rows are loaded as `tss`, already cleaned up to the dates. Turn the dates into real dates, find any that didn't fit, remove any outside the monitoring period, then count the samples in each season.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_dates
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
conc = pd.read_csv("data/yarrahappini_concentration.csv")
name = "Total suspended solids"
tss = conc[conc["Analyte"] == name].copy()
tss = tss[tss["Quality Code"] == 10]
tss = tss.dropna(subset=["Value"]).drop_duplicates()
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_dates
fmt = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M"
dates = pd.to_datetime(tss["Date Time"], format=fmt,
                       errors=______)
odd = tss.loc[dates.______(), "Date Time"]
print(odd)

fixed = pd.to_datetime(odd, format="mixed")
tss["Date"] = dates.fillna(fixed)
print("Earliest", tss["Date"].______())

tss = tss[tss["Date"] >= "2007-07-01"]

wet_months = [10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3]
is_wet = tss["Date"].dt.month.isin(______)
print(is_wet.sum(), "wet season samples")
print(len(tss) - is_wet.sum(), "dry season samples")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_dates"}
You want bad dates to become blanks, not errors. Then find the blanks, and the earliest date. The last gap is the list of wet months.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_dates"}
Use `errors="coerce"`, then `.isna()`, then `.min()`, then `wet_months`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_dates"}
```python
fmt = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M"
dates = pd.to_datetime(tss["Date Time"], format=fmt,
                       errors="coerce")
odd = tss.loc[dates.isna(), "Date Time"]
print(odd)

fixed = pd.to_datetime(odd, format="mixed")
tss["Date"] = dates.fillna(fixed)
print("Earliest", tss["Date"].min())

tss = tss[tss["Date"] >= "2007-07-01"]

wet_months = [10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3]
is_wet = tss["Date"].dt.month.isin(wet_months)
print(is_wet.sum(), "wet season samples")
print(len(tss) - is_wet.sum(), "dry season samples")
```
:::

What was the earliest date before you removed it? Why can't it be right?

## Your workbook code, copy from here

This is the code for Section 2 of your assessment workbook. It does every step on this page in order and prints how many rows each one removed. Run it here first, then copy it into your workbook.

It uses `my_site` and `my_analyte` from your Section 1 code, so run Section 1 first. The lines marked **your decision** are the ones to think about and change if you choose to.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: workbook_code
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
conc = pd.read_csv("data/yarrahappini_concentration.csv")
my_site = "145014A"
my_analyte = "Total nitrogen as N"
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: workbook_code
#| caption: Your workbook code
# Tidy stray spaces
clean = conc.copy()
for col in ["Site Code", "Analyte", "Unit", "Operator"]:
    clean[col] = clean[col].str.strip()

# Your site and pollutant
is_site = clean["Site Code"] == my_site
is_analyte = clean["Analyte"] == my_analyte
clean = clean[is_site & is_analyte].copy()
print(len(clean), "rows to start")

# Quality codes (your decision)
keep_codes = [10]
before = len(clean)
clean = clean[clean["Quality Code"].isin(keep_codes)]
print(before - len(clean), "removed by quality code")

# Blank values
before = len(clean)
clean = clean.dropna(subset=["Value"])
print(before - len(clean), "removed as blank")

# "<" values (your decision). To drop them,
# remove the # from the start of the next line.
# clean = clean[clean["Operator"] != "<"]
lt = (clean["Operator"] == "<").sum()
print(lt, "rows below the detection limit kept")

# Units
is_ug = clean["Unit"] == "Micrograms/Litre"
print(is_ug.sum(), "values converted from micrograms")
ug_values = clean.loc[is_ug, "Value"]
clean.loc[is_ug, "Value"] = ug_values / 1000
clean.loc[is_ug, "Unit"] = "Milligrams/Litre"

# Duplicates
before = len(clean)
clean = clean.drop_duplicates()
print(before - len(clean), "removed as duplicates")

# Dates, month first, then fix the odd ones
fmt = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M"
dates = pd.to_datetime(clean["Date Time"], format=fmt,
                       errors="coerce")
odd = clean.loc[dates.isna(), "Date Time"]
print("Dates that didn't fit")
print(odd)
fixed = pd.to_datetime(odd, format="mixed")
clean["Date"] = dates.fillna(fixed)

# Dates outside the monitoring period (your decision)
first_date = "2007-07-01"
before = len(clean)
clean = clean[clean["Date"] >= first_date]
print(before - len(clean), "removed as out of range")

# Seasons
wet_months = [10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3]
clean["Season"] = "Dry"
is_wet = clean["Date"].dt.month.isin(wet_months)
clean.loc[is_wet, "Season"] = "Wet"
wet = clean[clean["Season"] == "Wet"]
dry = clean[clean["Season"] == "Dry"]
print(len(wet), "wet and", len(dry), "dry samples")
```

The first step uses a short `for` loop to tidy four columns in one go. It does exactly what the four separate lines did in section 3. In your workbook you don't need the `pd.read_csv()` line, because `conc` is already loaded.
